title: In the Room: Things You Can Touch
overview:
Name the things around you.
Ask: what is this?
Say a and an before a thing.
Ask for a thing you need.
functions: Name the things in a room
Say a or an before a thing
Ask for a thing you need
Say what you have with you
Say thank you when you are given a thing
learningPath: Words: things in the room and in your pocket.
Patterns: a and an, and asking for a thing.
Write about what is in your bag.
Practice and quiz. Check your answers.
lectureScript:
This is Unit 6. Look around you.
Today you name the things you can see.
A book. A bag. A chair. A table.
Say them with me. Book. Bag. Chair. Table.
A door. A window. A desk. A box.
Say them with me.
Now the things in your pocket.
A key. A phone. Money. A card.
A bottle. A watch.
Say them with me.
Now a small word. Very small, and you need it.
In English you do not say: I have book.
You say: I have a book.
A comes before a thing.
But listen to this one.
An apple. An egg. An hour.
Before a, e, i, o and u, say an.
A book. An apple. Hear it?
It is easier to say. That is why.
Now, asking. This is the useful part.
You need a pen. You say: a pen, please.
Or: Can I have a pen, please?
Somebody gives it to you. You say thank you.
And the question: What is this?
Point at a thing. Ask: What is this?
That is Unit 6. Go and name things.

grammar.title: A and an
grammar.explanation:
English does not let you name one thing alone.
You need a small word first.
Almost always a. Sometimes an.
grammar.rule:
a book    a bag    a chair    a table
an apple  an egg   an hour    an old bag

an goes before the sounds a, e, i, o, u
a goes before everything else
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say you own an egg.
1. The word is egg.
2. Does it start with a, e, i, o or u? Yes, e.
3. So use an.
4. Say: I have an egg.
5. Now try bag. It starts with b, so: a bag.
grammar.mistake:
Many languages have no word here at all.
English needs one.
No: I have book.
Yes: I have a book.
grammar.tip: an before a, e, i, o, u. a before the rest.
grammar.practice:
Write a or an.
1. ___ book
2. ___ apple
3. ___ chair
4. ___ egg
5. ___ key
6. ___ hour
7. ___ table
8. ___ old bag
9. ___ phone
10. ___ window
grammar.answers:
1. a
2. an
3. a
4. an
5. a
6. an
7. a
8. an
9. a
10. a
Eight or more right? Good. Hour is strange: the h is silent.

grammar.title: What is this?
grammar.explanation:
One question names anything.
You never have to be stuck for a word.
grammar.rule:
What is this?
It is a book.

What is that?
It is a window.

Do not know the word?
Ask: What is this thing?
grammar.workedExample:
You see a thing. You have no word for it.
1. Point at it.
2. Ask: What is this?
3. They say: It is a bottle.
4. Say it back: A bottle.
5. Now you have the word. Write it down.
grammar.mistake:
Do not say who for a thing.
Who is for people.
What is for things.
grammar.tip: Point first, then ask. Pointing is not rude here.
grammar.practice:
What or who?
1. ___ is this? It is a key.
2. ___ is this? This is my sister.
3. ___ is that thing?
4. ___ is at the door?
grammar.answers:
1. What
2. Who
3. What
4. Who
All four? You can ask about anything now.

grammar.title: Asking for a thing
grammar.explanation:
Three ways, from short to polite.
All three work.
The longer one is safer with a stranger.
grammar.rule:
Short:   A pen, please.
Middle:  Can I have a pen, please?
Long:    Could I have a pen, please?

They give it to you.
You say: Thank you.
grammar.workedExample:
You are at a desk and you need a pen.
1. Start with can I have.
2. Then the thing: a pen.
3. Then please.
4. Say: Can I have a pen, please?
5. They give it. Say: Thank you.
grammar.mistake:
Do not say only: Pen.
One word alone sounds like an order.
Please changes everything.
grammar.practice:
Ask for these three ways is fine.
1. a pen
2. a chair
3. some water
4. the key
grammar.answers:
Any polite form is right.
Check: did you say please every time?
Did you use a or the correctly?
Water takes some, not a: some water.

grammar.title: What I have with me
grammar.explanation:
One verb says what is in your bag.
I have. You have. She has.
grammar.rule:
I have a key.
You have a phone.
He has a card.
She has a bag.
We have money.

he and she → has
everybody else → have
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say your sister owns a phone.
1. Your sister is she.
2. she goes with has.
3. Then the thing: a phone.
4. Say: She has a phone.
5. For yourself it is have: I have a phone.
grammar.mistake:
No: She have a phone.
Yes: She has a phone.
Only he, she and it take has.
grammar.tip: He and she take has. Everyone else takes have.
grammar.practice:
Write have or has.
1. I ___ a key.
2. She ___ a bag.
3. We ___ money.
4. He ___ a phone.
5. You ___ a book.
6. They ___ two boxes.
grammar.answers:
1. have
2. has
3. have
4. has
5. have
6. have
Five or six right? Good.

readings.title: What Is in My Bag
readings.genre: One person listing what they carry
readings.setting: On a bus, looking in a bag
readings.passage:
This is my bag.
It is not big.
I have a book in it.
I have a bottle of water.
I have my keys and my phone.
I have a card for the bus.
I have no money today.
That is all.
My bag is light.

readings.title: Can I Have a Pen?
readings.passage:
Excuse me. Can I have a pen, please?
Yes, of course. Here you are.
Thank you.
And a paper?
Here. Take one.
Thank you very much.
What is this word?
It is your name. Write it here.
Thank you.

readings.title: What to Bring
readings.genre: A notice on a classroom door
readings.setting: A door in an adult class
readings.passage:
Bring these things:
a pen
a book
a bag

Do not bring food.
Put your phone in your bag.
Thank you.

comprehension.a: A book, a bottle, keys, a phone and a card.

comprehension.q: Is there money in the bag?
comprehension.why: Line 7: I have no money today.
The last line: My bag is light.

comprehension.q: What does the person ask for first?
comprehension.why: Line 1: Can I have a pen, please?

comprehension.q: What do they ask for next?
What does the person say after they get the pen?
What could you say to ask for a chair?
comprehension.a: Can I have a chair, please?
comprehension.why: The talk uses the same pattern for a pen.

comprehension.q: How many things must you bring?
comprehension.why: A pen, a book and a bag.
The notice says: Do not bring food.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Point and name
speaking.instructions:
Look around you. Find these things.
Point at each one and name it.
1. a door
2. a window
3. a chair
4. a table
5. a bag
6. a book
Tap the mic. Say all six.
Say a or an before each one.
Tap again. Listen back.
Check: did you say a before every thing?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to name three things. Point at them if they are near you.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — What is this?
speaking.instructions:
Read A. Say B.
1. A: (points at a book) B: What is this?
2. A: It is a book. B: A book. Thank you.
3. A: (points at a window) B: What is that?
4. A: It is a window. B: A window. Thank you.
Tap the mic. Say the four B lines.
Check: did you say the word back to check it?
speaking.tutor: Point at three things and ask the tutor what each one is.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — What I have with me
speaking.instructions:
Say four lines about your bag or your pocket.
1. I have a (thing).
2. I have a (thing).
3. I have no (thing).
4. My bag is (big, small, heavy or light).
Tap the mic. Say the four lines.
Check: a or an before each thing?
speaking.tutor: Tell the tutor three things you have with you. Ask what it has.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Ask for a thing
speaking.instructions:
Read A. Say B.
1. A: Yes? B: Excuse me. Can I have a pen, please?
2. A: Here you are. B: Thank you.
3. A: Anything else? B: Yes. Can I have some water, please?
4. A: Of course. B: Thank you very much.
Tap the mic. Say the four B lines.
Check: please in both asks?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for three things. Use can I have and please each time.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — A or an?
speaking.instructions:
Tap Listen. Say a or an before each word.
1. book
2. apple
3. key
4. egg
5. table
6. hour
Tap the mic. Say six answers.
Check: a, an, a, an, a, an.
Hour is strange. The h is silent, so it sounds like our.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for three words that take an.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — The th in this and thing
speaking.instructions:
Listen and repeat.
this ... that ... thing ... three
Your tongue goes between your teeth.
It is not s. It is not t.
Now say these lines.
What is this thing?
This is my bag.
Tap the mic. Say both lines.
Check: can you feel your tongue?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say thing and sing. Say which one you heard.

writing.title: Writing 1 — What is in my bag
writing.prompt:
Write four lines.
Say what is in your bag.
Use a or an in each line.
writing.model:
I have a book.
I have a phone.
I have an apple.
I have no money.
writing.criteria:
Four lines.
a or an in each one.
Each line starts with a capital.
Each line ends with a full stop.
writing.extension: Add a line about what is NOT in your bag.

writing.title: Writing 2 — A list of things
writing.prompt:
Write a list of six things in this room.
One on each line.
Put a or an before each one.
writing.model:
a door
a window
a chair
a table
a book
an apple
writing.criteria:
Six things.
One on each line.
a or an before each one.
They are all really in the room.
writing.extension: Now write which one is nearest to you.

activities.instructions:

2. You read it. ___

4. You carry things in it. ___
5. You look out of it. ___

activities.answers:
1. a chair
2. a book
3. a door
4. a bag
5. a window
6. a key
7. a watch

Six or more right: good.
Note: money does not take a.
activities.solo: Say your answers out loud first.

activities.title: Practice 2 — What is this?
activities.instructions:
Point at six things near you.
For each one, ask and answer.
What is this? It is a ___.
Do it for a thing you cannot name.
Ask: What is this thing?
activities.answers:
There is no key here.
Check: did you ask before you answered?
Did you use a or an?
Did you write down any new word?
activities.solo: Record all six, then listen back.

activities.title: Practice 3 — A or an?
activities.instructions:
Write a or an.
1. ___ book
2. ___ egg
3. ___ table
4. ___ apple
5. ___ key
6. ___ hour
7. ___ window
8. ___ old box
9. ___ phone
10. ___ desk
activities.answers:
1. a
2. an
3. a
4. an
5. a
6. an
7. a
8. an
9. a
10. a
Eight or more right: good.
Hour takes an because the h is silent.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Ask for it
activities.instructions:
Ask for each thing. Use please.
1. a pen
2. a chair
3. some water
4. the key
5. a book
6. some paper
activities.answers:
Any polite form is right.
Can I have a pen, please? is a good model.
Check: please in all six?
Water and paper take some, not a.
activities.solo: Say all six out loud, then check.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Have or has
activities.instructions:
Write have or has.
1. I ___ a key.
2. She ___ a bag.
3. He ___ a phone.
4. We ___ money.
5. They ___ two boxes.
6. You ___ a book.
activities.answers:
1. have
2. has
3. has
4. have
5. have
6. have
Five or six right: good. Only he, she and it take has.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Read the notice
activities.instructions:
Read the notice again.
1. How many things must you bring?
2. Name them.
3. What must you not bring?
4. Where must your phone go?
5. Is a bottle on the list?
activities.answers:
1. Three
2. A pen, a book, a bag
3. Food
4. In your bag
5. No
Four or five right: you can read a notice. That is a real skill.
activities.solo: Read it, then answer without looking.

quizzes.q: You sit on it. It is a ___.
quizzes.why: A chair is for sitting. A table is for putting things on.

quizzes.q: You open a door with it. It is a ___.
You do not know the word. What do you ask?
quizzes.why: What asks about a thing. Who asks about a person.

quizzes.q: Which word is for a person, not a thing?

quizzes.why: Book starts with b, so a.
Apple starts with a vowel sound, so an.
Hour sounds like our. The h is silent, so an.

quizzes.q: What is the politest way to ask?
options: Can I have a pen, please?
quizzes.a: Can I have a pen, please?
quizzes.why: One word alone sounds like an order. Please changes it.

quizzes.q: A person gives you a pen. You say ___.
quizzes.why: Thank you is for when you get a thing.
He, she and it take has. Everyone else takes have.

quizzes.q: Which one is on the notice: bring a ___.
quizzes.why: The notice lists a pen, a book and a bag.

quizzes.q: More than one box is two ___.
quizzes.why: Box adds es, not just s.

teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card has a worked example, every practice has a key, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back, check.

teacherNotes.type: Everything here can be pointed at
teacherNotes.note: That is the design. Every word in this unit names something in the room or in a pocket, so a learner with no shared language can still be taught it and can still show you they know it. Use real objects rather than pictures wherever you can.

teacherNotes.type: A and an is small and it is not optional
teacherNotes.note: Many languages have no article at all, so a learner will drop it for a long time and be perfectly understood. It still marks their English as beginner. Correct it gently and often rather than heavily and once.

teacherNotes.type: What is this thing? is the escape hatch
teacherNotes.note: A learner who knows that one question is never stuck. It is worth more than any ten nouns, because it is how they get the other nouns for themselves. Make sure they leave the unit able to say it without thinking.
An hour looks wrong and sounds right. Say plainly that the rule is about the SOUND, not the letter, and the exception becomes a rule instead of a puzzle.

selfAssessment.statement: I can name the things in a room.
I can ask what a thing is.
I can use a and an.
I can ask for a thing I need.
I can say what I have with me.
I can find a thing on a list.

assignment.title: Name it, and ask for it
assignment.instructions:
Two parts.
1. Record yourself. Name six things you can see.
Say a or an before each one.
Then ask for two things politely.
2. Write four lines about what is in your bag.
Listen back before you finish.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and a written page
